prompt.brief: Design a distributed API rate limiter that enforces tenant, user, credential, IP, and endpoint quotas with predictable burst behavior, low overhead, and safe degradation.
successSignals: Define quota identity, policy precedence, token/refill semantics, burst capacity, response headers, time source, and scope inheritance.
Partition counters by policy key, isolate hot tenants/endpoints, and choose strict versus approximate enforcement for multi-region traffic.
Keep the decision path bounded and atomic; handle clock skew, retries, failover, counter loss, policy updates, and cache stampedes.
Explain fail-open/closed choices by endpoint risk, abuse resistance, observability, auditability, and degraded local limits.

functional: Evaluate requests against hierarchical quotas, return allow/deny/retry-after metadata, and support fixed, sliding, and token-bucket policies.
Manage plans and overrides, apply endpoint/tenant/user/IP dimensions, expose usage, and support distributed or regional enforcement.
Make decisions safe under retries, expire counters, audit policy changes, protect trusted traffic, and recover from limiter-store failure.
nonFunctional: Keep limiter decision p99 overhead under 10ms for the normal path and make endpoint-specific degradation explicit.
Handle 1M decisions per second and hot public endpoints without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Distributed API rate limiter commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Distributed API rate limiter writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Distributed API rate limiter version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Distributed API rate limiter by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Distributed API rate limiter work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Distributed API rate limiter projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Distributed API rate limiter projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Distributed API rate limiter records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Distributed API rate limiter latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
